title: RoFormer: Rotary Position Embedding (Su et al., 2021)
authoring_note: Anchors follow sources.json: rope:§x / rope:eqN / rope:pN for the paper, README.md:Lx for the official pseudocode, lecture_03.pdf:pNN for the CS336 slides. Section, equation and page numbers were verified against page images (discovered.json records which). Status 'computed' marks equations, 'implemented' code, 'shown' figures/tables, 'supplement' prerequisites the paper assumes. The shared-shift KP keeps id rope-relative-position because engine/fixtures/rope_shared_shift.json already back-references that id. Prompts follow commit-before-reveal; numeric answers were computed with 4blue2brown/cs336/models/rope.mjs.

knowledge_points.label: The requirement: score depends on positions only through m−n
knowledge_points.statement: RoPE asks for functions f_q, f_k such that ⟨f_q(x_m,m), f_k(x_n,n)⟩ = g(x_m, x_n, m−n): each of q and k is built from its own absolute position, yet their inner product may depend on positions only through the difference.

anchors.quote: ⟨f_q(x_m, m), f_k(x_n, n)⟩ = g(x_m, x_n, m − n)
we hope that the inner product encodes position information only in the relative form
all these approaches attempt to modify Equation (6) based on the decomposition of Equation (3)
a relative position embedding should be some 𝑓(𝑥, 𝑖) s.t. 𝑓 𝑥, 𝑖 , 𝑓 𝑦, 𝑗 = 𝑔(𝑥, 𝑦, 𝑖 − 𝑗) ... That is, the attention function only gets to depend on the relative position (i-j)

provenance.filtering_note: The paper reaches Eq. 11 through a two-page lineage of additive schemes (Eqs. 3-10: Vaswani, Shaw, Transformer-XL, T5, DeBERTa). The course compresses that lineage into three bullets on p31 (sine has cross terms, absolute is not relative, relative is not an inner product) and states the requirement first. Basis: evidence from both sources.

misconceptions.belief: A relative encoding means f itself takes m−n as input.
misconceptions.why_wrong: f_q sees only m and f_k only n (Eq. 1); relativity is a property of the inner product, not of the per-token function. That is what makes the scheme usable with a cache and with linear attention.

predict.q: Sinusoidal encoding adds p_m to x_m before the projection. Expand ⟨W_q(x_m+p_m), W_k(x_n+p_n)⟩ into four terms. Which terms depend on an absolute position (m or n) rather than only on m−n?
predict.answer: The two cross terms x_m^T W_q^T W_k p_n and p_m^T W_q^T W_k x_n, and the pure term p_m^T W_q^T W_k p_n is not a function of m−n either after the projections; only the content term x_m^T W_q^T W_k x_n is position-free.
predict.why: Addition before projection produces cross terms mixing one token's content with the other token's absolute position (Eq. 6, and lecture p31 'various cross-terms that are not relative'). Eq. 11 demands that no such absolute dependence survive. Note the distinction: the bare sinusoidal dot product p_m·p_n = Σ cos θ_i(m−n) is relative; it is the projection W_q^T W_k sitting between the two position vectors that mixes frequencies and brings back absolute (m+n) terms.

transfer.q: A colleague proposes f_q(x,m) = W_q x + m·u and f_k(x,n) = W_k x + n·u for a fixed vector u. Name the position-position term in ⟨f_q, f_k⟩ that violates the requirement of Eq. 11 (the cross terms violate it too).
transfer.answer: m·n·u^T u (and the cross terms m·u^T W_k x_n, n·x_m^T W_q^T u): a product m·n is not a function of m−n.
transfer.why: Any additive position term produces a bilinear position-position term; m·n cannot be rewritten as a function of m−n. Multiplicative (rotational) coupling is what avoids it.

check.q: Let c > 1 be a constant and u a fixed vector. Under Eq. 1, f_q may see only (x_m, m) and f_k only (x_n, n). Which pair satisfies Eq. 11, i.e. makes the real inner product <f_q, f_k> depend on positions only through m − n?
choices: f_q = c^m · W_q x_m and f_k = c^(−n) · W_k x_n
f_q = c^m · W_q x_m and f_k = c^n · W_k x_n
f_q = W_q x_m + m·u and f_k = W_k x_n − n·u
f_q = (m − n) · W_q x_m and f_k = W_k x_n
check.answer: f_q = c^m · W_q x_m and f_k = c^(−n) · W_k x_n
check.why: <c^m W_q x_m, c^(−n) W_k x_n> = c^(m−n) x_m^T W_q^T W_k x_n, a function of x_m, x_n and m − n only (Eq. 11), and each function uses only its own position (Eq. 1). c^m and c^n give c^(m+n). The additive pair gives cross terms m·u^T W_k x_n and −n·x_m^T W_q^T u plus −m·n·u^T u, none a function of m − n. (m − n)·W_q x_m makes f_q depend on n, which Eq. 1 forbids. (This scaling solution is unbounded, which is why the paper uses unit-modulus rotations, but it meets the stated requirement.)

distractor_from.f_q = c^m · W_q x_m and f_k = c^n · W_k: Same-sign coupling: positions add (m + n) instead of subtracting, the error the conjugate/transposed rotation avoids.
distractor_from.f_q = W_q x_m + m·u and f_k = W_k x_n −: Additive position terms, which always leave cross terms and an m·n term.
distractor_from.f_q = (m − n) · W_q x_m and f_k = W_k x_: Misconception: a relative encoding means f itself takes m − n as input.

check.targets_misconception: A relative encoding means f itself takes m−n as input.
check.varies: Multiplicative scalar coupling and a menu of candidate f's instead of diagnosing one additive proposal (functional: recognise a valid solution, not a violating term).
check.invariant: Each token's function uses only its own position, and the position dependence must cancel to m − n inside the inner product; opposite-sign multiplicative coupling does this, additive terms cannot.

retrieval.q: Write the functional requirement RoPE places on q_m = f_q(x_m,m) and k_n = f_k(x_n,n).
Which of the two functions, f_q or f_k, receives the relative offset m−n as an argument?
retrieval.answer: Neither; each receives only its own absolute position. m−n appears only in the inner product g.

prompts.self_explain: Why would a method that needs m−n inside f_k be a problem for a decoder that caches keys?

steps.do: Test each scheme on p31 against Eq. 11's two conditions: (a) the score is an inner product of a query built from (x_m, m) alone and a key built from (x_n, n) alone; (b) positions enter only through m−n.
steps.why: Eq. 11 asks for both at once, and each earlier scheme on the slide fails exactly one of them.

steps.do: Sinusoidal vectors added before the projection: ⟨W_q(x_m+p_m), W_k(x_n+p_n)⟩ is an inner product, but its expansion contains cross terms such as x_mᵀW_qᵀW_k p_n that depend on n by itself. Fails (b).
steps.why: The bilinear form distributes over each sum, so content gets paired with an absolute position (p31: 'various cross-terms that are not relative').

steps.do: Learned absolute embeddings: the same additive form with p_m read from a table. Fails (b).
steps.why: Nothing ties a free table entry p_m to a difference of positions, so the position terms are absolute (p31: absolute is not relative).

steps.do: Relative embeddings: a learned term indexed by i−j is added to the score. Passes (b), fails (a).
steps.why: The position term is added next to the inner product instead of being part of it, so the score is no longer ⟨f_q, f_k⟩ of per-token vectors (p31: not an inner product). Eq. 11 asks for a scheme that passes both tests.

knowledge_points.label: Supplement: 2D rotations preserve dot products and add angles
knowledge_points.statement: A 2D rotation R(α) is orthogonal (R^T R = I), so it preserves norms and dot products, and rotations compose by adding angles: R(α)R(β) = R(α+β) and R(α)^T = R(−α).

anchors.quote: Note that R^d_Θ is an orthogonal matrix, which ensures stability during the process of encoding position information.
We know that inner products are invariant to arbitrary rotation.
return [c*v[0]-s*v[1], s*v[0]+c*v[1]]

provenance.filtering_note: Both the paper and the course use R_m^T R_n = R_{n−m} without stating it; the paper says only 'R is orthogonal'. The additive-angle identity is the step that actually produces n−m, so the student line adds it as an assumed prerequisite (author inference).

misconceptions.belief: Rotating both vectors by different angles keeps the dot product unchanged because rotation preserves it.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Invariance holds for the same rotation applied to both; different angles leave a net rotation of α−β between them.

predict.q: q = (1,0) and k = (0.7,0.7). Rotate q by 30° and k by 90°. What is the norm of the rotated q, and what is the angle between the rotated vectors?
predict.answer: Norm stays 1; the angle between them is 45° + 60° = 105° (rotation by 30° and 90° opens the original 45° gap by 60°).
predict.why: Rotation is orthogonal so lengths do not change; the relative angle changes by the difference of the two rotation angles only.

transfer.q: Instead of rotating q by α and k by β, you rotate only q by α−β and leave k alone. How does the dot product compare with the two-rotation case?
transfer.why: R(α)q · R(β)k = q^T R(α)^T R(β) k = q^T R(β−α) k = (R(α−β) q)^T k. Only the difference matters and it can be moved onto either vector.

check.q: q = (2, 0) and k = (0, 3), so q · k = 0. Rotate q by 100° and k by 40° (both counter-clockwise). What is the dot product of the rotated vectors? Give the number to two decimals.
check.why: R(α)q · R(β)k = q^T R(β − α) k. Equivalently, q now points at 100° and k at 90° + 40° = 130°, so the angle between them is 30° and the norms 2 and 3 are unchanged: 2 · 3 · cos 30° = 6 · 0.8660 = 5.196. Checked with rope.mjs dot(rotate([2,0],100°), rotate([0,3],40°)) = 5.19615.
check.targets_misconception: Rotating both vectors by different angles keeps the dot product unchanged because rotation preserves it.
check.varies: Different vectors and angles, with an originally orthogonal pair, asking for the numeric dot product rather than a comparison (functional: compute the effect of the angle difference).
check.invariant: Rotations are orthogonal and compose by adding angles, so only the difference β − α changes the dot product.

retrieval.q: Simplify R(α)^T R(β) for 2D rotation matrices.
What property of R(α) guarantees that ‖R(α)v‖ = ‖v‖?

presentations.notice: The lengths of both arrows never change, whatever the angles; only the gap between them moves the readout.
Whatever α and β are, both arrows keep their lengths, and R(α)q · R(β)k always equals q · R(β−α)k. Only the difference β − α moves the dot product.

knowledge_points.label: Supplement: multiplying by e^{iθ} is a rotation; Re[z w*] is a dot product
knowledge_points.statement: Identifying (a,b) with z = a + ib, multiplication by e^{iθ} rotates z by θ, and Re[z w*] equals the real dot product of the two 2-vectors, so Re[z e^{imθ} (w e^{inθ})*] = Re[z w* e^{i(m−n)θ}].

anchors.quote: g(x_m, x_n, m−n) = Re[(W_q x_m)(W_k x_n)* e^{i(m−n)θ}]
f_q(x_q, m) = R_q(x_q, m) e^{iΘ_q(x_q, m)}
Just pair up the coordinates and rotate them in 2d (motivation: complex numbers)

provenance.filtering_note: The paper moves between the complex form (Eq. 12) and the matrix form (Eq. 13) in one sentence and never states the Re[z w*] = dot-product identity. The course names complex numbers only as a 'motivation' on p33. Author inference that this is the missing bridge.

misconceptions.belief: z w (no conjugate) gives the dot product.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Re[z w] = ac − bd; the conjugate flips the sign of the second term so Re[z w*] = ac + bd. Without the conjugate the phases add instead of subtract and m+n appears, not m−n.

predict.q: z = 1 + 0i (the vector (1,0)) and w = 0.7 + 0.7i. Compute Re[z e^{iπ/6} (w e^{iπ/2})*] to two decimals.
predict.why: The phases combine to e^{i(π/6 − π/2)} = e^{−iπ/3}. Re[w* e^{−iπ/3}] with w* = 0.7 − 0.7i gives 0.7cos(π/3) − 0.7sin(π/3) = 0.35 − 0.606 = −0.256. Same as rotaryPair().before in rope.mjs.

transfer.q: Same z, w, but you forget the conjugate and compute Re[z e^{iπ/6} w e^{iπ/2}]. Which combined phase appears, and is the result still a function of m−n?
transfer.answer: Phase e^{i(π/6 + π/2)} = e^{i2π/3}; the result depends on m+n, so it is no longer relative.
transfer.why: Conjugation negates the key's phase; that negation is exactly what turns the sum of positions into a difference.

check.q: Take z = 2 + i (the query pair) and w = 1 − i (the key pair), positions m = 3 and n = 1, and θ = π/3. Compute Re[z e^{imθ} (w e^{inθ})*], where * is complex conjugation. Give the number to two decimals.
check.why: Re[z e^{imθ} (w e^{inθ})*] = Re[z w* e^{i(m−n)θ}]. z w* = (2 + i)(1 + i) = 1 + 3i. e^{i·2π/3} = −0.5 + 0.8660i. (1 + 3i)(−0.5 + 0.8660i) has real part −0.5 − 3 · 0.8660 = −3.098. Equivalently the dot product of (2,1) rotated by π and (1,−1) rotated by π/3 (rope.mjs gives −3.0981). Forgetting the conjugate gives Re[z w e^{i4π/3}] = Re[(3 − i)(−0.5 − 0.866i)] = −2.366, which the tolerance rejects.
check.targets_misconception: z w (no conjugate) gives the dot product.
check.varies: Non-unit complex numbers, different positions and frequency (functional: carry out the conjugate-and-subtract computation numerically).
check.invariant: Re[a b*] is the 2D dot product, and conjugating the key negates its phase so positions enter as m − n.

retrieval.q: For 2-vectors written as complex numbers z and w, which complex expression equals their real dot product?
retrieval.answer: Re[z w*] (real part of z times the conjugate of w)

retrieval.q: Multiplying a complex number by e^{iθ} does what to the corresponding 2-vector?
retrieval.answer: Rotates it counter-clockwise by θ, preserving its length

steps.do: Multiplying z = a + ib by e^{iφ} rotates the 2-vector (a, b) by φ.
steps.why: The real and imaginary parts are exactly the 2×2 rotation matrix of Eq. 13 applied to (a, b).

steps.do: With w = c + id, the real part of z w* is the dot product (a, b)·(c, d).
steps.why: Conjugating w flips the sign of d, so the cross terms bc − ad land in the imaginary part and only ac + bd is real.

steps.do: Rotate the query by mθ and the key by nθ, then take Re: this is Eq. 12's g.
steps.why: The conjugate of a product is the product of conjugates, and (e^{inθ})* = e^{−inθ}, so the key's phase enters with a minus sign and the two positions meet only as m − n.

steps.do: The predict's numbers: z = 1, w = 0.7 + 0.7i, phases π/6 and π/2. z w* e^{−iπ/3} = (0.7 − 0.7i)(0.5 − 0.866i), real part 0.35 − 0.606 = −0.256.
steps.why: Same value as rotating (1, 0) by 30° and (0.7, 0.7) by 90° and taking the dot product (rope.mjs rotaryPair().before), as step 2 says it must be.

presentations.notice: With the key conjugated, the complex readout equals the dot product and its phase is α − β. Untick the conjugate: the phase becomes α + β and the readout no longer matches the dot product.

knowledge_points.label: The 2D solution: rotate the projected vector by mθ
knowledge_points.statement: In d = 2 the requirement is met by f_q(x_m,m) = (W_q x_m) e^{imθ} and f_k(x_n,n) = (W_k x_n) e^{inθ}, i.e. rotate the projected query by angle mθ and the projected key by nθ, giving g = Re[(W_q x_m)(W_k x_n)* e^{i(m−n)θ}].

anchors.quote: f_q(x_m, m) = (W_q x_m) e^{imθ}
f_{q,k}(x_m, m) = [[cos mθ, −sin mθ],[sin mθ, cos mθ]] W_{q,k} x_m
φ(m) = mθ + γ
the angular functions does not dependent on query and key ... φ(m) with continuous integer inputs produce an arithmetic progression
Rotate we by ‘0 positions’ ... know by ‘1 positions’

provenance.filtering_note: §3.2.1 presents Eq. 12 as 'a solution' and defers the derivation to §3.4.1, where polar decomposition plus the initial condition at position 0 forces the radius to be position-free and the angle to be an arithmetic progression φ(m) = mθ + γ (Eqs. 24-30). The course (p32) gives only the picture 'rotate by the position' and never shows that rotation is forced rather than merely sufficient. The paper itself proves sufficiency and a form of necessity only under its extra assumptions (Eqs. 22, 28).

misconceptions.belief: The rotation angle depends on the token content x_m.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Eq. 28: Θ_f(x, m) = φ(m) + θ_x, and the content-dependent part cancels between query and key at m = n (Eq. 26b); only mθ survives.

predict.q: θ = π/6, W_q x_m = (1,0) at m = 1, W_k x_n = (0.7,0.7) at n = 3. Compute the RoPE score q_m^T k_n to two decimals.
predict.why: q rotates by 30° to (0.866, 0.5); k rotates by 90° to (−0.7, 0.7); dot product = −0.606 + 0.35 = −0.256 (rope.mjs rotaryPair().before).

transfer.q: Swap the positions: the query is now at m = 3 and the key at n = 1, contents unchanged. Compute the score to two decimals.
transfer.why: Now the relative rotation is R(n−m) = R(−60°): k rotated by −60° gives (0.956, −0.256), dot with (1,0) is 0.956. The score depends on the sign of m−n, not only its magnitude, so RoPE distinguishes 'key before query' from 'key after query'.

retrieval.q: In the 2D case, by what angle is the projected query at position m rotated?
retrieval.answer: mθ, with θ a fixed non-zero constant

retrieval.q: Which two facts about f does the paper's 2D derivation extract from the initial condition at position 0 and the m = n case?
retrieval.answer: The radial part is position-independent (‖q‖, ‖k‖), and the angle is φ(m) + θ_{q,k} with φ an arithmetic progression mθ + γ

prompts.self_explain: Why does setting m = n in Eq. 24 tell you the radius cannot depend on position?

steps.do: Write the query and key functions in polar form (Eq. 23), with the initial condition q = f_q(x_q, 0), k = f_k(x_k, 0).
steps.why: A product of complex numbers multiplies radii and adds angles, so polar form splits the requirement into one condition on radii and one on angles.

steps.do: Eq. 24: the radii must multiply, and the angles subtract, to functions of n − m only.
steps.why: The score pairs the query with the conjugate of the key, so the key's angle enters with the opposite sign.

steps.do: Set n = m. Then R_q(x_q,m)R_k(x_k,m) = R_g(x_q,x_k,0) = ‖q‖‖k‖ and Θ_k(x_k,m) − Θ_q(x_q,m) = θ_k − θ_q, where θ_q, θ_k are the angles of q and k.
steps.why: With equal positions the right-hand sides no longer depend on m, so they equal their values at m = 0, the unrotated q and k.

steps.do: The paper takes the radius to be position-free, R_q(x_q,m) = ‖q‖, R_k(x_k,n) = ‖k‖. The angle condition rearranges to Θ_q(x_q,m) − θ_q = Θ_k(x_k,m) − θ_k, so both sides equal one function φ(m) of the position alone.
steps.why: The left side depends on x_q only and the right side on x_k only; they can be equal for all inputs only if neither depends on the input.

steps.do: Put n = m + 1 in the angle condition: the step φ(m+1) − φ(m) is the same for every m, which gives Eq. 30.
steps.why: The right-hand side does not contain m, and a sequence with a constant step is an arithmetic progression.

steps.do: With γ = 0 and q = W_q x_m this is Eq. 33, the 2D solution of Eq. 12: rotate the projected query by mθ (and the key by nθ).
steps.why: The radius and the input angle rebuild q itself; the only thing position adds is the angle mθ, so the encoding is a rotation.

presentations.notice: The faint-arrow readout q_m · k_n depends only on n − m: move m and n up by the same amount and it stays put, while changing just one of them changes it.

knowledge_points.label: d dimensions: block-diagonal rotations with θ_i = 10000^{−2i/d}
knowledge_points.statement: For even d, split the vector into d/2 adjacent pairs and rotate pair i by mθ_i, with θ_i = 10000^{−2(i−1)/d} for i = 1..d/2, so R^d_{Θ,m} is block-diagonal with 2×2 rotations at geometrically spaced frequencies from 1 down to about 10000^{−1}.

anchors.quote: f_{q,k}(x_m, m) = R^d_{Θ,m} W_{q,k} x_m
Figure 1: Implementation of Rotary Position Embedding(RoPE).
Following Vaswani et al. [2017], we set θ_i = 10000^{−2i/d}.
There are many rotations, which one do you pick? ... Just pair up the coordinates and rotate them in 2d
rotate([vector[i],vector[i+1]], position*base**(-i/vector.length))

provenance.filtering_note: The paper writes the exponent two ways: 10000^{−2(i−1)/d} with i from 1 (Eq. 15) and 10000^{−2i/d} in §3.3 and §3.4.3 (i from 0). They describe the same set; the atlas uses the 0-indexed form to match rope.mjs. The paper does not motivate the choice beyond 'following Vaswani et al.'; the course (p33) adds that Gemma 4 rotates only the first two coordinates as an alternative, which the paper does not discuss. The paper says nothing about why pairs are adjacent rather than (i, i+d/2).

misconceptions.belief: All pairs rotate by the same angle mθ.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Each pair has its own θ_i; with one shared θ every position m and m + 2π/θ would collide, and the model could not resolve distances at more than one scale.

predict.q: d = 8 with base 10000. List the four frequencies θ_0..θ_3 (0-indexed, θ_i = 10000^{−2i/d}).
predict.why: 10000^{−2i/8} = 10^{−i}: the frequencies form a geometric sequence, so pair 0 turns a full radian per position while pair 3 turns a thousandth of a radian.

transfer.q: Apply block-diagonal RoPE with d = 4 to the vector (1, 0, 1, 0) at position m = 2. Give the second pair (coordinates 3 and 4) to three decimals.
transfer.why: Pair 1 has θ_1 = 10000^{−2/4} = 0.01, so it rotates by 0.02 rad: (cos 0.02, sin 0.02) = (0.9998, 0.0200). The first pair rotates by 2 rad to (−0.416, 0.909). rope.mjs rotatePairs([1,0,1,0], 2).

check.q: RoPE with d = 6 and base 10000 (θ_i = 10000^{−2(i−1)/d}, i = 1..3). At position m = 500, by what angle in radians is the third pair (coordinates 5 and 6) rotated? Give the number to three decimals.
check.why: The third pair has i = 3, so θ_3 = 10000^{−4/6} = 10000^{−2/3} = 0.0021544. The rotation angle is mθ_3 = 500 × 0.0021544 = 1.0772 rad. rope.mjs rotatePairs([0,0,0,0,1,0], 500) returns (0.4738, 0.8806) for that pair, whose angle atan2(0.8806, 0.4738) = 1.0772.
check.targets_misconception: All pairs rotate by the same angle mθ.
check.varies: A different d (6, so non-decade frequencies), a large position, and the low-frequency pair instead of a d = 4 coordinate output (functional: compute one pair's angle from Eq. 15).
check.invariant: Pair i rotates by m·θ_i with θ_i = 10000^{−2(i−1)/d}, geometrically spaced across pairs.

retrieval.q: For head dimension d, how many independent 2×2 rotation blocks does R^d_{Θ,m} contain?
Write RoPE's rotation frequency θ_i, saying how i is counted.
retrieval.answer: θ_i = 10000^{−2i/d}, i counted from 0 (Eq. 15 writes the same set as 10000^{−2(i−1)/d}, i = 1..d/2)

prompts.self_explain: What would a learner lose if all d/2 blocks used the same θ?

steps.do: Split the d-vector into d/2 adjacent pairs (x_1, x_2), (x_3, x_4), … and rotate pair i by mθ_i.
steps.why: Each pair is a 2D plane where the 2D solution (Eq. 13) applies on its own, so the d-dimensional rotation is d/2 independent 2D ones.

steps.do: Eq. 15 counts pairs from 1; §3.3 and rope.mjs count from 0.
steps.why: Same set of frequencies with the index shifted by one: the first pair has θ = 1 and the last 10000^{−(d−2)/d}, close to 1/10000.
Consecutive pairs differ by the constant factor 10000^{2/d} (here 10), so the frequencies form a geometric sequence from fast to slow.

presentations.notice: At the same position, pair 1 has turned many times while the last pair has barely moved. On the log axis θ_i lies on a straight line, so each pair is slower than the one before by the same factor.

knowledge_points.label: Shared shift cancels: q_m^T k_n = q^T R_{n−m} k
knowledge_points.statement: Because R_m^T R_n = R_{n−m}, the rotary score (R_m W_q x_m)^T (R_n W_k x_n) = x_m^T W_q^T R_{n−m} W_k x_n depends on positions only through n−m; shifting both positions by the same s leaves it unchanged.

anchors.quote: q_m^T k_n = (R^d_{Θ,m} W_q x_m)^T (R^d_{Θ,n} W_k x_n) = x^T W_q R^d_{Θ,n−m} W_k x_n
where R^d_{Θ,n−m} = (R^d_{Θ,m})^T R^d_{Θ,n}
a = tf.einsum('bjhd,bkhd->bhjk', qw, kw)
We want our embeddings to be invariant to absolute position
before:dot(qm,kn), after:dot(qs,ks), relative:dot(q,rotate(k,(n-m)*theta))

provenance.filtering_note: The paper asserts (R_m)^T R_n = R_{n−m} without proof; it follows block-by-block from the additive-angle identity (supplement KP). The course states the goal ('invariant to absolute position', p32) with a picture of 'we know' shifted by two positions but does not write Eq. 16.

misconceptions.belief: Because rotation preserves dot products, the score is the same as without RoPE.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Rotation preserves the score only when both vectors get the same rotation; here they get mθ and nθ, so a net R_{n−m} remains, and that is the point.
R_{n−m} and R_{m−n} are transposes, not equal; the score at (m,n) = (1,3) is −0.26 while at (3,1) it is +0.96 in the fixture.

retrieval.answer: q_m^T k_n = x_m^T W_q^T R_{n−m} W_k x_n

steps.why: The transpose of a product reverses the order, so the two rotations end up next to each other between the projections.

steps.do: Work block by block.
steps.why: A rotation is orthogonal, so its transpose is the rotation by the opposite angle, and rotations compose by adding angles (supp-rotation-preserves-dot).

steps.do: Collect the blocks: this is Eq. 16 (§3.2.2).
steps.why: Block-diagonal matrices multiply block by block, and every block i uses the same θ_i in R_m and R_n.

knowledge_points.label: Multiplicative rotation vs additive position vectors
knowledge_points.statement: Additive schemes (Eqs. 3-10) put position into the expanded score as extra terms that must then be edited or removed; RoPE multiplies q and k by rotations so relative position appears inside the one content term and no cross terms exist.

anchors.quote: In contrast to the additive nature of position embedding method adopted in the previous works, i.e., Equations (3) to (10), our approach is multiplicative.
q_m^T k_n = x_m^T W_q^T W_k x_n + x_m^T W_q^T W_k p_n + p_m^T W_q^T W_k x_n + p_m^T W_q^T W_k p_n
Difference with sine embeddings – not additive, no cross terms
Relative embeddings: add a vector to the attention computation ... T5, Gopher, Chinchilla

provenance.filtering_note: The paper's related-work section attributes each edited term to its predecessor (Shaw: relative key vector; Transformer-XL: sinusoid + u, v; T5: scalar bias; DeBERTa: drop the p-p term). The course keeps only the taxonomy on p30 and the one-line contrast on p34, dropping the per-method equations.

misconceptions.belief: RoPE is 'the sinusoidal encoding applied to q and k instead of x'.
misconceptions.why_wrong: It uses the same frequencies but multiplies (rotates) rather than adds; adding sinusoids to q and k would recreate the cross terms of Eq. 6.

predict.q: Expand the RoPE score (R_m q)^T (R_n k) for d = 2. How many terms involve the content of only one of the two tokens?
predict.why: The product collapses to q^T R_{n−m} k, a single bilinear form in q and k; there is no separate position vector to pair with one token's content.

transfer.q: T5 replaces the four terms of Eq. 6 with x_m^T W_q^T W_k x_n + b_{i,j} (Eq. 8). Which feature of Eq. 11's requirement does T5 satisfy and which does RoPE add on top of it?
transfer.answer: T5's score depends on positions only through the learned bias b_{i−j} (satisfies relativity), but it is not an inner product of a per-token q and k, so it cannot be used with linear attention or written as ⟨f_q, f_k⟩; RoPE keeps the inner-product form.
transfer.why: Lecture p31 notes relative embeddings are 'not an inner product'; the paper's §1 makes the same point as the reason for linear-attention compatibility.

check.q: A codebase labels as 'RoPE' a scheme that adds sinusoidal vectors after the projection: q_m = W_q x_m + p_m and k_n = W_k x_n + p_n. Expand q_m^T k_n into its four terms. How many of those terms pair one token's content with the other token's position vector? Type only the number.
check.why: q_m^T k_n = x_m^T W_q^T W_k x_n + x_m^T W_q^T p_n + p_m^T W_k x_n + p_m^T p_n. The two middle terms each combine one token's content with the other token's position p_n or p_m: 2 terms, the same cross-term structure as Eq. 6. True RoPE, (R_m W_q x_m)^T (R_n W_k x_n) = x_m^T W_q^T R_{n−m} W_k x_n, has one term and zero cross terms (§3.2.2: 'our approach is multiplicative').
check.targets_misconception: RoPE is 'the sinusoidal encoding applied to q and k instead of x'.
check.varies: Sinusoids added after projection (to q and k) rather than RoPE's own score, counting cross terms in the impostor (functional: inverse case of the predict prompt).
check.invariant: Adding position vectors always produces content-position cross terms; multiplying by rotations puts position inside the single content term.

retrieval.q: In one word each: how do the position encodings the paper reviews before RoPE inject position, and how does RoPE inject it?

Which encoding leaves the four-term expansion of the query-key score, with absolute position added to each embedding, with cross terms between one token's content and the other's absolute position: sinusoidal-additive or RoPE?
choices: Sinusoidal-additive
RoPE

steps.tex: q_m^\top k_n = x_m^\top W_q^\top W_k x_n + x_m^\top W_q^\top W_k p_n + p_m^\top W_q^\top W_k x_n + p_m^\top W_q^\top W_k p_n
steps.do: Additive absolute encoding (Eq. 3) gives q_m = W_q(x_m + p_m), k_n = W_k(x_n + p_n); expanding their inner product gives Eq. 6.
steps.why: The bilinear form distributes over both sums, so every pairing of content and position becomes its own term.

steps.do: Only the first term is free of position. The two middle terms pair one token's content with the other token's absolute position; the last pairs the two positions.
steps.why: These three terms are what Eqs. 7-10 edit one at a time to make the score relative: Transformer-XL swaps p_n for a relative sinusoid and p_m for trained vectors u, v; DeBERTa drops the position-position term.

steps.tex: (R_m W_q x_m)^\top (R_n W_k x_n) = x_m^\top W_q^\top R_{n-m} W_k x_n
steps.do: RoPE multiplies instead of adding: the score is a single term.
steps.why: §3.2.2 calls the approach multiplicative: relative position sits inside the content term as R_{n−m}, so there are no cross terms to edit (lecture p34: 'no cross terms').

knowledge_points.label: Long-term decay: the bound on the rotary score falls with distance
knowledge_points.statement: Writing the rotary score as Re Σ_i q_i k_i^* e^{i(m−n)θ_i} and applying Abel summation bounds it by (max_i |h_{i+1} − h_i|) · Σ_i |S_{i+1}| with S_j = Σ_{i<j} e^{i(m−n)θ_i}; with geometric θ_i the average |S_i| decreases with |m−n|, which the paper offers as the 'long-term decay' property.

anchors.quote: Figure 2: Long-term decay of RoPE.
One can prove that this setting provides a long-term decay property ... the inner-product will decay when the relative position increase.
Note that the value of (1/(d/2)) Σ |S_i| decay with the relative distance m − n increases by setting θ_i = 10000^{−2i/d}, as shown in Figure (2).

provenance.filtering_note: What is proved (Eq. 37) is an upper bound whose distance-dependent factor is Σ|S_i|; that this factor decays is asserted by plot (Fig. 2), not proved, and the plot shows an oscillating envelope, not monotone decay. The actual score for particular q, k can be large at large distance. §3.3 phrases it as 'the inner-product will decay', which overstates Eq. 37. Lecture 3 does not cover this property at all; the course treats RoPE as a relative encoding and moves on.

misconceptions.belief: RoPE makes attention scores shrink with distance for every query-key pair.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Only the Abel bound's distance factor Σ|S_i| decays on average; the content factor max|h_{i+1} − h_i| is arbitrary and a model can learn q, k that attend far away.

predict.q: In Eq. 37 the score's magnitude is bounded by a product of two factors. Which factor carries the dependence on m−n, and which carries the dependence on the token contents q, k?
predict.answer: Σ_i |S_{i+1}| carries m−n (S_j sums e^{i(m−n)θ_i}); max_i |h_{i+1} − h_i| carries the contents (h_i = q_i k_i^*).
predict.why: Abel summation separates the content sequence h_i from the phase partial sums S_j; only the phases know the distance.

transfer.q: Suppose all θ_i were set equal to a single θ. What does S_j = Σ_{i<j} e^{i(m−n)θ} do as m−n grows, and what happens to the claimed decay?
transfer.answer: S_j = j·e^{i(m−n)θ} has constant magnitude j for every distance, so Σ|S_i| does not decay at all; the decay relies on the spread of frequencies so that the phases dephase and partially cancel.
transfer.why: Decay in Fig. 2 comes from summing rotating unit phasors at many different rates; with one rate there is no cancellation.

check.q: After training, one RoPE attention head reliably puts a large score on a token 300 positions back. How does this observation relate to the paper's long-term decay result (Eqs. 35-37, Fig. 2)?
choices: No conflict: only an upper bound's distance factor decays, and learned q, k can still score high
A conflict: RoPE forces every query-key score to fall steadily as the relative distance grows
No conflict: the decay result only applies to distances longer than the model's training length
A conflict, unless the head has learned to make all of its frequencies θ_i equal during training
check.answer: No conflict: only an upper bound's distance factor decays, and learned q, k can still score high
check.why: Eq. 37 bounds |score| by (max_i |h_{i+1} − h_i|) · Σ_i |S_{i+1}|; only the second factor depends on m − n, and §3.4.3 says its average (1/(d/2)) Σ|S_i| decays with distance. The content factor depends on the learned q and k, so a particular pair can still have a large score at distance 300. The bound is not distance-restricted to beyond training length, and θ_i are fixed by Eq. 15, not learned.

distractor_from.A conflict: RoPE forces every query-key: Misconception: RoPE makes attention scores shrink with distance for every query-key pair.
distractor_from.No conflict: the decay result only appli: Invents a scope restriction; the analysis says nothing about training length.
distractor_from.A conflict, unless the head has learned: Treats θ_i as learned and misreads equal frequencies (which remove the decay) as the escape route.

check.targets_misconception: RoPE makes attention scores shrink with distance for every query-key pair.
check.varies: An empirical observation about a trained head instead of a modified frequency schedule (domain: interpreting the bound against learned behaviour).
check.invariant: The decay is of a bound's distance factor (average |S_i|), multiplied by an unconstrained content factor; it limits nothing pair-by-pair.

retrieval.q: Which summation technique does the paper use to turn Σ h_i e^{i(m−n)θ_i} into a bound with separate content and distance factors?
To show RoPE's long-term decay, what quantity does the paper plot against relative distance?

prompts.self_explain: Why is a decaying upper bound weaker evidence than a decaying score?

steps.tex: (R^d_{\Theta,m}W_q x_m)^\top(R^d_{\Theta,n}W_k x_n) = \mathrm{Re}\Big[\sum_{i=0}^{d/2-1} h_i\, e^{i(m-n)\theta_i}\Big],\quad h_i = q_{[2i:2i+1]}k^*_{[2i:2i+1]}
steps.do: Eq. 35: read each pair as one complex number, so the score is a sum of d/2 rotated products.
steps.why: Per pair this is the 2D score Re[q k* e^{i(m−n)θ}] of Eq. 12; the block-diagonal form just adds the pairs up.

steps.tex: S_j = \sum_{k=0}^{j-1} e^{i(m-n)\theta_k},\quad S_0 = 0,\quad h_{d/2} = 0,\quad e^{i(m-n)\theta_i} = S_{i+1}-S_i
steps.do: Define the partial sums of the phases and write each phase as a difference of two of them.
steps.why: This is Abel summation (summation by parts): it moves the dependence on distance from single phases, which never shrink, into the partial sums, which can cancel.

steps.do: Eq. 36: regroup by S_{i+1}.
steps.why: Each S_j appears once with +h_{j−1} and once with −h_j; the boundary terms vanish because S_0 = 0 and h_{d/2} = 0.

steps.do: Eq. 37: triangle inequality, then pull out the largest content difference.
steps.why: The first factor depends only on q and k; the second only on m − n and the θ_i, so all the distance dependence is in Σ|S_{i+1}|, the quantity Fig. 2 plots.

presentations.notice: The relative bound falls from (d/2 + 1)/2 at distance 0 and keeps rippling. With 'all θ_i equal' it stays flat. With the aligned pair shown, one score still peaks at r0 under the decaying bound.

knowledge_points.label: Efficient realization: elementwise cos/sin instead of a d×d matmul
knowledge_points.statement: Because R^d_{Θ,m} is block-diagonal, R x = x ⊙ (cos mθ_1, cos mθ_1, cos mθ_2, ...) + (−x_2, x_1, −x_4, x_3, ...) ⊙ (sin mθ_1, sin mθ_1, ...): two elementwise products on q and k, after which attention is the ordinary einsum.

anchors.quote: due to the sparsity of R^d_Θ, applying matrix multiplication directly as in Equation (16) is not computationally efficient
cos_pos = repeat_elements(sinusoidal_pos[..., None, 1::2], rep=2, axis=-1)
qw2 = stack([-qw[..., 1::2], qw[..., ::2]], 4) ... qw = qw * cos_pos + qw2 * sin_pos
build_transformer_model(config_path, ..., model='roformer', ...)
The actual RoPE math: Multiply with sines and cosines
Get the RoPE matrix cos/sin; Multiply query/key inputs

provenance.filtering_note: The official repo does not contain the rotary layer; train.py:L122 only selects model='roformer' from bert4keras, and README.md:L18-L32 is the authors' pseudocode (snapshot in code_snapshots/rope_readme_excerpt.py). The paper and README pair adjacent coordinates (−x_2, x_1); many later implementations (and CS336 assignment code) pair coordinate i with i + d/2 ('rotate_half'), which is the same operator under a fixed permutation of dimensions. The course shows the implementation (p35) without Eq. 34.

misconceptions.belief: RoPE needs a d×d matrix multiply per token, so it is expensive.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The matrix has only two non-zeros per row; Eq. 34 turns it into 2d multiplies and d adds per vector, cheaper than the projection W_q x itself.

predict.q: d = 4, x = (x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4). Write the 'companion' vector that gets multiplied by the sin terms in Eq. 34 (the README's qw2).
predict.why: Each pair (a, b) rotated by φ is (a cos φ − b sin φ, a sin φ + b cos φ); collecting the sin coefficients gives (−b, a). README.md:L24 builds it with stack([-qw[..., 1::2], qw[..., ::2]]).

transfer.q: An implementation pairs coordinate i with i + d/2 instead of adjacent coordinates and uses companion (−x_{d/2+1..d}, x_{1..d/2}). For d = 4 with the same θ_1, θ_2, what permutation of the paper's coordinates makes the two implementations compute the same scores?
transfer.answer: Map paper order (x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4) to (x_1, x_3, x_2, x_4): pair (1,2) becomes (1,3) and pair (3,4) becomes (2,4); since the same permutation is applied to q and k the dot product is unchanged.
transfer.why: Both are block-diagonal rotations with the same frequencies; a fixed permutation applied to both q and k commutes with the dot product.

check.q: Using Eq. 34 (x ⊙ cos-vector + companion ⊙ sin-vector) to rotate one vector with d = 96, how many scalar multiplications are needed? Count only the two elementwise products: the cos and sin values are precomputed and the sign flips that build the companion vector are not multiplications. Type only the number.
check.why: Eq. 34 computes x ⊙ (cos mθ_1, cos mθ_1, ...) and (−x_2, x_1, ...) ⊙ (sin mθ_1, sin mθ_1, ...): two elementwise products of length d, so 2d = 192 multiplications (plus d additions). Applying the dense R^d_{Θ,m} as in Eq. 16 would take d^2 = 9216, though each row has only two non-zeros (§3.2.2: 'due to the sparsity of R^d_Θ ... not computationally efficient').
check.targets_misconception: RoPE needs a d×d matrix multiply per token, so it is expensive.
check.varies: A cost count at a new d instead of a coordinate-pairing permutation (functional: quantify the sparsity Eq. 34 exploits).
check.invariant: R^d_{Θ,m} is block-diagonal with 2×2 blocks, so R x reduces to two elementwise products with cos/sin vectors.

retrieval.q: How many multiplications does RoPE's elementwise cos/sin form use to rotate one d-dimensional vector, compared with a dense d×d matmul?
In the official README pseudocode, what is computed after qw and kw are rotated?
retrieval.answer: The ordinary attention einsum 'bjhd,bkhd->bhjk' between rotated qw and kw

prompts.self_explain: Why do cos_pos and sin_pos repeat each frequency twice along the last axis?

steps.do: Rotate the first pair with Eq. 13's matrix.
steps.why: R^d_{Θ,m} is block-diagonal, so each pair is rotated on its own and nothing outside the pair is touched.

steps.do: Split each output coordinate into its cos part and its sin part.
steps.why: Both coordinates have one cos term and one sin term, so the pair is two elementwise products; the sin factor multiplies the swapped pair with one sign flipped.

steps.tex: R^d_{\Theta,m}x = x\otimes(\cos m\theta_1,\cos m\theta_1,\cos m\theta_2,\cos m\theta_2,\dots)^\top + (-x_2,x_1,-x_4,x_3,\dots)^\top\otimes(\sin m\theta_1,\sin m\theta_1,\dots)^\top
steps.do: Repeat for every pair with its own θ_i: this is Eq. 34.
steps.why: Each frequency is repeated twice because it serves both coordinates of its pair. The cos and sin vectors depend only on m, so they are computed once and reused (README.md:L22-L29 builds cos_pos, sin_pos and qw2).

knowledge_points.label: RoPE is applied to q and k inside every attention layer, not at the embedding
knowledge_points.statement: Rotation is applied to the projected query and key (W_q x, W_k x) in each attention operation, never to the input embedding once, and never to the value.

anchors.quote: Note: embedding at each attention operation to enforce position invariance
f_{q,k}(x_m, m) = R^d_{Θ,m} W_{q,k} x_m
we replace the sinusoidal position encoding in the self-attention block of the baseline model with our proposed RoPE and realizes self-attention according to Equation (16)

provenance.filtering_note: The paper never says 'every layer' in §3; it is implicit in Eq. 14 being applied to W_q x and stated only in the experimental setup (§4.2.2). The course makes it an explicit note on p35. The value vector is left unrotated in both (Eq. 2 uses v_n directly; the README rotates only qw and kw).

misconceptions.belief: RoPE rotates the token embedding once at the input like sinusoidal encoding.
misconceptions.why_wrong: A rotation of x before residual layers would be scrambled by the non-linear blocks; the relative-position identity holds only if R multiplies the q and k that enter the very dot product.

predict.q: In a 12-layer Transformer with RoPE, how many times is the rotation applied to a token's representations during one forward pass, counting query and key separately?
predict.why: Once for q and once for k in each of the 12 attention layers; the values and the input embedding are never rotated.

transfer.q: An engineer rotates q, k and also v to 'be consistent'. Which quantity in Eq. 2 changes as a result, and does the relative-position identity of Eq. 16 still hold?
transfer.answer: The output o_m = Σ a_{m,n} v_n changes because each v_n is now rotated by nθ (absolute position leaks into the output); Eq. 16 for the scores a_{m,n} still holds since it involves only q and k.
transfer.why: The identity is about the inner product; the value path is a weighted sum, where a position-dependent rotation is not cancelled by anything.

check.q: An engineer removes RoPE from attention and instead rotates each token embedding once, x'_m = R_m x_m, before layer 1. In layer 1 the score is (W_q x'_m)^T (W_k x'_n). What happens to relative-position dependence in that layer?
choices: Kept in layer 1 only; it is lost from layer 2 onward because the MLPs are non-linear
Kept: rotations preserve inner products, so the score still depends only on m − n here
Lost: W_q and W_k sit between R_m and R_n, so the rotations no longer merge into R_(n−m)
Kept only if W_q equals W_k, since then the projection cancels and leaves R_(n−m)
check.answer: Lost: W_q and W_k sit between R_m and R_n, so the rotations no longer merge into R_(n−m)
check.why: (W_q R_m x_m)^T (W_k R_n x_n) = x_m^T R_m^T W_q^T W_k R_n x_n. R_m^T R_n = R_(n−m) only when the rotations are adjacent; general W_q^T W_k does not commute with rotations, so the score depends on m and n separately. Eq. 14 applies R to W x for this reason, and lecture p35 notes RoPE is applied 'at each attention operation'. Even W_q = W_k does not make W^T W commute with R in general.

distractor_from.Kept: rotations preserve inner products,: Over-applies rotation invariance while ignoring the projections in between.
distractor_from.Kept in layer 1 only; it is lost from la: Misconception: RoPE rotates the embedding once at the input like sinusoidal encoding, failing only later through non-linear blocks.
distractor_from.Kept only if W_q equals W_k, since then: Assumes W^T W is a scalar or commutes with rotations whenever the projections are equal.

check.targets_misconception: RoPE rotates the token embedding once at the input like sinusoidal encoding.
check.varies: Rotation moved to the embedding instead of extended to the value (functional: a different misplacement of R).
check.invariant: The relative identity R_m^T R_n = R_(n−m) needs the rotations to act on the very q and k that enter the dot product.

knowledge_points.label: RoPE inside linear attention: rotate the feature maps in the numerator
knowledge_points.statement: In kernelized attention Σ_n φ(q_m)^T φ(k_n) v_n / Σ_n φ(q_m)^T φ(k_n), RoPE is inserted as (R_m φ(q_m))^T (R_n φ(k_n)) in the numerator only, leaving the denominator unrotated; this is possible because rotation does not change norms, but the numerator may then contain negative weights.

anchors.quote: Attention(Q,K,V)_m = Σ_n (R_m φ(q_m))^T (R_n φ(k_n)) v_n / Σ_n φ(q_m)^T φ(k_n)
Attention(Q,K,V)_m = Σ_n φ(q_m)^T φ(k_n) v_n / Σ_n φ(q_m)^T φ(k_n)

we keep the denominator unchanged to avoid the risk of dividing zero, and the summation in the numerator could contain negative terms ... we kindly argue that the computation can still model the importance of values
previous relative position encoding-based approaches are not compatible with linear self-attention

provenance.filtering_note: The paper asserts without proof that the non-normalized, possibly negative weights 'can still model the importance of values'; the only support is the Performer+RoPE convergence curve (Fig. 3). Lecture 3 does not mention linear attention or this property; the course covers RoPE for softmax attention only.

misconceptions.belief: The rotated weights in Eq. 19 still sum to one over n.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The denominator uses unrotated features, so the numerator weights are neither normalized nor non-negative; the paper says so explicitly.

predict.q: Linear attention requires φ(q)^T φ(k) ≥ 0 so that weights are a valid mixture. After inserting R_m and R_n into the numerator as in Eq. 19, which sign constraint is lost and where does the paper put the rotations to keep the denominator safe?
predict.answer: Non-negativity of the per-key weights is lost (rotated features can have negative inner products); the rotations are applied only in the numerator, and the denominator keeps the unrotated φ(q)^T φ(k) so it cannot be zero.
predict.why: Rotation preserves norms but not sign of inner products; keeping the unrotated positive denominator avoids division by zero.

transfer.q: Why can an additive relative bias b_{m−n} (T5-style) not be inserted into Eq. 18 in the same way RoPE is inserted into Eq. 19?
transfer.answer: Linear attention needs the score to factor as φ(q_m)^T φ(k_n) so that Σ_n φ(k_n) v_n^T can be precomputed; an additive term b_{m−n} inside a softmax-free score does not factor into a per-query and a per-key part, whereas R_m φ(q_m) and R_n φ(k_n) do.
transfer.why: RoPE keeps the inner-product form (KP rope-position-goal); that factorization is exactly what linear attention exploits.

check.q: 2D linear attention with RoPE as in Eq. 19, θ = π/3, R_p rotating by pθ. Query at m = 1 with φ(q) = (1, 0); keys φ(k_0) = (1, 0) at n = 0 and φ(k_1) = (0.6, 0.8) at n = 1. Each key's effective weight is its rotated numerator term divided by the shared unrotated denominator Σ_n φ(q)^T φ(k_n). What is the sum of the two effective weights? Give the number to two decimals.
check.why: Numerator terms: (R_1 φ(q))^T (R_n φ(k_n)) = φ(q)^T R((n−1)θ) φ(k_n). n = 0: R(−π/3)(1,0) = (0.5, −0.866), dot (1,0) = 0.5. n = 1: R(0), dot = 0.6. Denominator (unrotated): 1 + 0.6 = 1.6. Sum = (0.5 + 0.6)/1.6 = 0.6875. The weights do not sum to 1 because the denominator is not rotated (§3.3). Checked with rope.mjs.
check.targets_misconception: The rotated weights in Eq. 19 still sum to one over n.
check.varies: A concrete numeric instance of Eq. 19 instead of a factorization argument about additive biases (functional: compute the normalization defect).
check.invariant: Eq. 19 rotates only the numerator's feature maps and keeps the unrotated denominator, so effective weights are neither normalized nor guaranteed non-negative.

retrieval.q: When RoPE is inserted into linear (kernelized) attention, which part of the fraction is rotated: numerator, denominator, or both?
choices: Numerator only
Denominator only
Both

retrieval.q: What property of R lets the paper multiply the non-negative feature maps by the rotation without changing their magnitude?

steps.do: Eq. 18: linear attention with non-negative feature maps.
steps.why: With φ ≥ 0 every weight and the denominator are positive, and because the score splits into a query part and a key part, Σ_n φ(k_n) v_nᵀ can be summed once and reused for every query.

steps.do: Eq. 19 rotates the feature maps in the numerator.
steps.why: R_n φ(k_n) still depends on token n alone, so the precomputed sum survives, and Eq. 16 makes the numerator relative.

steps.do: The denominator stays Σ_n φ(q_m)ᵀφ(k_n), unrotated.
steps.why: §3.3: rotated products can be negative, so a rotated denominator could reach zero; the unrotated one stays positive. What is given up is that the numerator weights may be negative and no longer form a normalized mixture.

presentations.notice: The unrotated denominator stays positive, but with θ > 0 and the query at a different position from the keys the effective weights stop summing to 1. A key whose rotated term turns negative (key 1 once (n − m)θ passes 90°) gets a negative weight.

knowledge_points.label: What the experiments showed and did not show
knowledge_points.statement: The paper reports 27.5 vs 27.3 BLEU on WMT14 En-De (Table 1), faster MLM-loss convergence for RoFormer and for Performer+RoPE (Fig. 3, curves only), mixed GLUE results (Table 2: better on MRPC/STS-B/QQP, worse on SST-2/QNLI/MNLI), and 69.79 vs 68.29 accuracy on CAIL2019-SCM at length 1024 vs 512 (Table 5); none of these come with seeds, variance, or a test of extrapolation beyond training length.

anchors.quote: Transformer-base 27.3; RoFormer 27.5
Compare to the vanilla BERT, RoFormer experiences faster convergence.
RoFormer is higher on MRPC, STS-B, and QQP, but lower on SST-2, QNLI, and MNLI (bundle finding glue_task_deltas)
68.29 at length 512 and 69.79 at length 1024 (bundle finding long_sequence_legal)
Our experiments show that it consistently achieves better performance compared to its alternatives.
Rope embeddings ... GPTJ, PaLM, LLaMA, Most 2024+ models

provenance.filtering_note: The introduction claims 'consistently better performance'; Table 2 is mixed and Table 1's 0.2 BLEU gap has no variance estimate. 'Sequence length flexibility' is claimed in §1 but no experiment trains at one length and tests at another; Table 5 compares two training lengths. The course does not cite the paper's results at all: its evidence for RoPE is adoption (p30: GPT-J, PaLM, LLaMA, most 2024+ models) and its later note (p65) that long-range layers may drop RoPE (NoPE) while short-range layers keep RoPE with sliding windows. Basis: evidence for both the paper's numbers and the course's framing; the 'not shown' list is author inference from the absence of such experiments in §4.

misconceptions.why_wrong: No experiment tests a model beyond its training length; Table 5 trains separate 512 and 1024 models.

predict.q: Table 1 compares Transformer-base and RoFormer on WMT14 En-De. What is the BLEU difference, and how many runs per model does the paper report?
predict.answer: 0.2 BLEU (27.5 vs 27.3); one run each (single model from averaging the last 5 checkpoints), no seeds or variance.
predict.why: The result is reported as a single number per model in §4.1.2-4.1.3, which is below typical seed-to-seed variation on this benchmark.

transfer.q: A summary says 'RoFormer beats BERT on all GLUE tasks'. Using Table 2 as the paper reports it, name one task where that summary is wrong.
transfer.answer: Any of SST-2, QNLI, or MNLI (RoFormer is lower there); it is higher only on MRPC, STS-B and QQP.
transfer.why: The bundle's finding glue_task_deltas records Table 2 as mixed, contradicting the 'consistently better' wording of §1.

check.q: Which of these statements about RoFormer is supported by the results the paper reports?
choices: It beat BERT on every one of the six GLUE tasks reported in the paper's Table 2
A model trained at 512 tokens kept its accuracy when tested on 1024-token inputs
Its WMT14 En-De gain over Transformer-base exceeds the run-to-run variance shown
On CAIL2019-SCM, the 1024-length setting scored 1.5 points above the 512-length one
check.answer: On CAIL2019-SCM, the 1024-length setting scored 1.5 points above the 512-length one
check.why: Table 5 reports 68.29 at length 512 and 69.79 at length 1024: 69.79 − 68.29 = 1.50. No experiment evaluates beyond training length (Table 5 compares separate 512 and 1024 settings); Table 1 gives single numbers 27.5 vs 27.3 with no seeds or variance; Table 2 is mixed (lower on SST-2, QNLI, MNLI).

distractor_from.A model trained at 512 tokens kept its a: Misconception: the paper demonstrates length extrapolation.
distractor_from.Its WMT14 En-De gain over Transformer-ba: Assumes variance or seeds are reported; Table 1 is one number per model.
distractor_from.It beat BERT on every one of the six GLU: Takes §1's 'consistently better' wording at face value against the mixed Table 2.

check.varies: Selecting the one supported claim across four experiments instead of refuting a GLUE summary (domain: Table 5 and missing variance rather than Table 2).
check.invariant: Separate what each table actually measures (single runs, separate length settings, mixed GLUE) from the paper's broader claims.

retrieval.q: Which two GLUE tasks from {MRPC, SST-2, QNLI} does RoFormer score lower on than BERT?
What evidence does the RoFormer paper give for its 'faster convergence' claim?
retrieval.answer: Only plotted training-loss curves (Figure 3), not a table of numbers.

prompts.self_explain: Which of the three properties claimed in §1 (length flexibility, decay, linear-attention compatibility) is tested by an experiment in §4, and how?

path.note: Paper order: §2 lineage motivates §3.1 requirement, §3.2.1 2D solution, §3.2.2 general form and Eq. 16, §3.3 properties (decay, linear attention), §3.4.2 efficient realization, §4 experiments. Supplements are the two prerequisites the paper uses without stating.

course_path.note: Lecture 3 order (slides 30-35, then 65): taxonomy and requirement (p30-31), rotation invariance as the idea (p32), which rotation: pair coordinates (p33), the math and 'no cross terms' (p34), implementation at every attention layer (p35), later NoPE/SWA context (p65). The course never states Eq. 16 explicitly, skips long-term decay, linear attention and the paper's experiments, and uses adoption as evidence. Rotation invariance is said (p32) rather than assumed, so it is a stop here rather than a supplement.
